title: Breaking and Entering: Jazmine Mary on Art, Inner Critics and Radical Acts
transcript:
Jazmine Mary joined Lauren Taylor to talk about I Want to Rock and Roll, her album on Flying Nun, ahead of her show at the Merri Creek Tavern. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 11 June 2026.

Lauren: A pleasure to have you joining me on Breaking and Entering, Jazmine.

Jazmine: Thanks for having me.

Lauren: It's lovely to have you here. As well as playing tonight, you played over the weekend. We were just chatting about Rising's Day Tripper festival that you were a part of, which is kind of like a festival within a festival. Did you manage to stick around at Day Tripper and catch any of the other acts?

Jazmine: Yeah, I watched Kae Tempest. I'm a big fan. That was awesome. And Xiao Xiao was one of the other ones I watched the entire set of, which was really, really fun. I hadn't seen them before.

Lauren: Cool. And being in Melbourne for the last few days now: you're based in New Zealand now, but I was surprised to learn that you're originally from Australia. You grew up in…

Jazmine: Yeah, I grew up in Gippsland.

Lauren: In Gippsland. And you lived in Melbourne for a little while.

Jazmine: A couple of years, when I was like 18, 19. Had a bit too much fun.

Lauren: Being back here, are there things that you like to do, or places that are special to you, that you've returned to on this trip?

Jazmine: I was actually looking at Degraves Street or something, where I met my first girlfriend when I was like 18, and then the [name uncertain] next door, where she dumped me like six months later. It's okay. I'll be all right. It was a long time ago. But it was funny walking around and seeing these little places of baby me.

Lauren: I did see on stories you played in Ballarat yesterday as well. I saw that you stopped in at the iconic Pancake Parlour — Pancake Kitchen.

Jazmine: Yeah. [wording uncertain: “Well, you should have stopped out the front.”]

Lauren: Oh, you did. You didn't go in. I was going to ask you about your pancake order. But when did you make that move across the ditch to New Zealand? How long ago was that?

Jazmine: Maybe, like, I would have been 21, so, yeah, 2012 or something, or 14.

Lauren: It's quite a while ago. You've spoken about how you never really discovered a music community until you moved to Aotearoa. Can you tell me about that musical community you connected with, and what was it about the local scene and the environment there that finally made you feel connected?

Jazmine: I mean, I think Gippsland, Trafalgar specifically, the town I'm from, is so small. There's no bands, there's no music. And if there is, it was dudes in screamo bands, maybe, in like two towns over. So the idea of being a musician didn't even really exist, other than going on Australian Idol or something like that. Real small-town brain. And then moved to Melbourne and was just culture shocked. Little town kid, I was like, whoa, I felt so out of my depth. And like I said, just got up to a bunch of nonsense for a few years.

And so I think when I moved to New Zealand, I started to find community and people. I played guitar and stuff, but I think I found people there that were really encouraging. There's some experimental nights I'd go to and join in, and people just kept saying to play, or inviting me to, or collaborating. And it just slowly happened, and all of a sudden I was doing it all the time. So it was quite a lovely way to grow into a musician, I think.

Lauren: And you mentioned, when you're creating music, that you're extremely impulsive and intuitive. You create music quite quickly to stay ahead of your critical self, you said. Many creators, or just many people, get completely paralysed by their inner critic. Do you have any advice for artists who may want to learn how to move faster than their own self-doubt?

Jazmine: Yeah. I don't know if you have to move quickly to get away from self-doubt. But I think being around people that make you feel incredible. My band are really supportive, and all my friends, they will make me feel like I can do anything. And that's really nice, so they can lift me up really, really too high. And then my inner critic will smash me back down enough to sort of central. But having good people around you that are supportive, and that celebrate your wins, I think, is massive.

Lauren: Totally. Given you like to work in that really impulsive way, and enjoy improvisation as well, are there any happy accident moments that make their way onto this new album?

Jazmine: Oh, heaps of stuff. Even a lot of the production stuff is kind of going into the studio with 50% of the songs done, the bones of it, and then leaving space for improvisation, or things to change. I think a lot of the vocal things that happen, because I like to do one or two takes, a lot of the woos, or sometimes maybe I can hear myself smiling and things. Or just little ritual or practice to get into a present state while recording. That stuff that I can hear in the song that's quite nice, like a candle burning that I know is happening. Yeah, but lots of happy accidents.

Lauren: In terms of where you do a lot of your writing, you've said that you sing a lot in the car, and do a lot of voice memos in the car as well. Do you find the rhythm of driving, or just being alone in the car, helps the melodies or ideas flow better?

Jazmine: I think it's the only time I'm in quiet. I don't like listening to music in the car, really. And I think I have a really busy life, and I'm sure a lot of people relate to that, as when you're in the car, you're there, you're in your box, and you're flying down a highway, and you can't do anything else. So I feel like that's kind of when my mind creatively frees up, where I'm processing my thoughts and feelings, all of those things.

And no one can hear you. So scream singing, or sounding stupid, I don't know, there's a real protectiveness to the car, so that no one can catch you. It's too quick or something.

Lauren: Safe space. Do you have any daily rituals that are important to you in terms of your creative practice?

Jazmine: Maybe not daily. I just try and do it all the time. I write a lot when I'm in a connected space. If I'm connected to myself, I try and write a lot, which happens less when touring, because we're all in the car together, and then sleeping together, and then eating together. And I love it, but there's less time for creativity then. But yeah, going outside, being in nature, just all that cliché stuff. That's a cliché for a reason, you know. Anything that helps me listen to myself is going to help me be able to create.

Lauren: I wanted to bring up a really insightful article you wrote for Rolling Stone recently, which is for their Making Music, Making Ends Meet, a new series that they're focusing on musicians during the cost of living crisis. And you said, “To remain an artist is a radical act.” Can I ask, what is it about making music and art right now that makes it feel radical for you?

Jazmine: I think even a real conservative response to me saying, “To be an artist right now is a radical act,” is like, “No, it's not. Buckle up, what happened to rock and roll?” This is some of the boomer responses to this thing.

I think doing something hopeful and doing something meaningful, and that music and art is usually a space where people are wanting change: we're all playing fundraiser shows for a free Palestine. We're all activists. We're all trying to help free each other, and I don't really know many artists that aren't doing that. And to do that when getting paid fuck all, and being told you're ungrateful at the same time by a certain group of people, yeah, it is a radical act. And it's just radical to remain hopeful and loving. To be hopeless right now is a very powerful fascist tool. It's very indulgent to say, “Well, it's not going to do anything, so I won't do anything.” I think that's extremely lazy. And yeah, it's just brave to feel in this world, isn't it, right now?

Lauren: You've also said your art is a way to understand yourself, and also to be understood. And I'm curious, what did you learn about yourself through the making of your latest record?

Jazmine: Hmm. I think if I knew how to articulate that so well in words, I wouldn't write the music. So I don't know if I know how to articulate that exactly. And it's always changing, and I can't always mark it. I think I'm still in the process of learning what that is, but I think I'm just constantly getting kinder toward myself, which is no small feat, and therefore kinder to the world around me. Yeah, I don't know. I'm just getting closer to, I don't know, just having a fucking weird, nice time, you know?

Lauren: Yeah. Taking the right thing seriously and the other stuff not. That's a beautiful thing. You mentioned sharing your work and talking to people helps you get to understand what you're doing. When you're making it, you don't really understand what you're doing: kind of an interesting internal creation versus that external discovery. In a sense, does it feel like you're experiencing your own work for the first time only after you release it to everyone else?

Jazmine: I think it just changes. So it's like, it's mine, and I'm doing it, and experiencing whatever that is. And then as soon as you share it, it kind of becomes everyone else's, right? And then there's no way to ever go back to the source of creating it, because someone the other day was like, “I was so heartbroken, and I was listening to all of those songs.” And for them, that was that thing. That wasn't my — well, you know. So I think as soon as it leaves the body, it just takes on a million forms. And that's what's so cool about it, about anyone's art or music, right? Is that it can just kind of — the ownership goes.

Lauren: It's interesting how that dialogue with an audience can reveal meaning in your work. Does an artist need an audience to truly understand their own creation, do you think?

Jazmine: Nah, surely not, right? I don't think so. I'd hate to say that. No, I don't think so.

Lauren: I was intrigued when you said as well about your music that you like confusing people, but you also like feeling confused and figuring it out. Do you intentionally engineer moments of confusion to challenge yourself in any way? Do you enjoy problem solving, or being a puzzle, in a way?

Jazmine: No, God, no, it's all hard enough without putting effort into that. But I think it just goes back to acting on that impulse, and being like, it's art, so it can be really, really sincere, but it can also be a lie and be sincere at the same time. It's all made up and it's all real. And maybe the reason I talked about confusing people and being confused is because I get asked some very literal questions about things I do a lot, and find it really hard to know how to answer those without being boring. Like, “What does the album title mean?” And it's like, “Well, man, I don't know.”

Lauren: Lucky I didn't have that on my list of questions for you.

Jazmine: Yeah, no, well, I assumed not.

Lauren: I want to say a very big thank you to my guest, Jazmine Mary, who's been joining me today. You can catch Jazmine tonight at the Merri Creek Tavern, which should be a really special show. And you're off to Canberra tomorrow.

Jazmine: That's it. If you've got any friends there, please send them along.

Lauren: And do check out Jazmine Mary's amazing videos as well. They're really quite gorgeous. And we were chatting off air, saying there's a connection with the Bats with those videos.

Jazmine: Oh, Annabel Kean, yeah, whose parents are in the Bats. And Annabel does most of those videos with me. Does a great job.

Lauren: That's very cool. You've also mentioned each song on the record occupies its own emotional space. I've lined up the track 'Memphis' to play. What kind of emotional space would you say that this track occupies?

Jazmine: Oh, there's not normally a story, but that was at LynnMall, a West Auckland mall. And I was so fucking depressed. And I was crying, crying, crying in the car. And you know when you're in that void of such sadness, you don't know what to do with your body. So I went into the mall to get a mall massage. I was zombie, zombying through life; I didn't know what to do. And I went in to get this massage. And 'Walking in Memphis' was bleeding in through the mall, with this meditation music that was also on. And it was super trippy, because of my state. And I was laying on my back, and I opened my eyes, and the masseuse looked at me and said, “It's okay. I can see you now. You can relax.” And that just made me feel, I don't know. It was a very spiritual experience at the mall.

Lauren: I love that. This is 'Memphis' from Jazmine Mary. Thanks so much, Jazmine.

Jazmine: Thanks for having me.
